title: Electron Beam-Induced Formation of MWCNT-Ag Nanostructures in a Transmission Electron Microscope
content: Multi-walled carbon nanotubes (MWCNTs) have garnered significant attention in nanotechnology due to their exceptional mechanical, electrical, and chemical properties [1]. Their high surface area, excellent electrical conductivity, and structural stability make them ideal candidates for various applications, including catalysis, sensing, and energy storage. In particular, functionalization of MWCNTs with metal nanoparticles, such as silver nanoparticles (AgNPs), has been widely explored to enhance their catalytic and optical properties. Silver exhibits remarkable antimicrobial, plasmonic, and catalytic characteristics, which, when combined with MWCNTs, can lead to hybrid nanostructures with superior performance in diverse technological applications [2]. The deposition of AgNPs onto MWCNTs can be achieved through various synthesis techniques, including physical vapor deposition, electrochemical deposition, and chemical reduction. Among these, chemical reduction remains one of the most effective and scalable approaches, allowing for controlled nucleation and growth of AgNPs on the carbonaceous surface. The size, distribution, and morphology of AgNPs on MWCNTs are critical factors influencing their functional properties, which can be further tailored by post-synthetic modifications, such as thermal treatments or exposure to external stimuli [3]. One such external factor that can influence the structural and chemical properties of nanomaterials is electron beam irradiation. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) is a powerful tool for characterizing nanoscale materials, offering high spatial resolution imaging and in situ analysis capabilities. However, the high-energy electron beam used in TEM can induce structural transformations, atom migration, and even nanoparticle coalescence, which may significantly alter the morphology and distribution of metal nanoparticles on MWCNTs [4]. While these beam-induced effects are often considered an artifact during TEM imaging, they also present an opportunity for controlled modification of nanomaterials in situ. Understanding the interaction between electron beams and AgNP-decorated MWCNTs is crucial for both accurate material characterization and potential applications in nanofabrication [5].
